Before cutting both the springs are in series. They act as one. After you cut the rope they are in parallel. In first case the elongation of both springs is added together. In the second case it is not added its just the elongation of a single spring, hence when you cut it the weight moves up by value of the elongation of a single spring.

Total elongation in series = L +L = 2L

Total elongation in Parallel= L


Elongation After cutting - Elongation before cutting= L -2L= -L

Author: @DANGJOS
Content:
It's obvious that it's supposed to go up, given the build up in this short form video. As for why, I think it's somewhat straightforward. Pausing at 1:36, we can see the green rope is taut and pulling down on the spring above it and up on the spring below it, as strings/ropes do (I'm calling it a string from here on). The tension from the green string is stretching out both springs, and therefore making them *longer.* If you cut the string, the top spring will pull *up* on the black rope, and the bottom spring will pull *down* on the red rope. Because the top spring is attached to the anchor at the top, the top of the top spring and the red rope *cannot* move. This means that as the bottom spring pulls into itself the red rope will pull up on it and therefore up on the weight as well. The top spring will pull up on the black spring (as it pulls into itself) and therefore also pull up on the weight. This creates two *independent forces* pushing *up* on the weight at the bottom. 

If you think about it, this is the same as a linear or vertical double spring system versus a lateral spring system. In the former, you have two springs sharing the "work" of producing enough force to pull up the weight, and their stretch adds together, which reduces the effective spring constant. But in the latter (lateral system), the two springs pull *separately* on the weight, and therefore they stretch independently, which makes them overall shorter with the same force. I think that's the same thing that's happening here, expect they cleverly used ropes and string to switch between the two systems.

Hopefully I didn't screw anything up. I haven't seen the full video, but this is what makes sense to me

And F=kx=Tension
For series, 1/k(net) = 1/k1 + 1/k2
For parallel, K(net) = k1 + k2
So, Tension force in parallel > Tension force in series. 
Therefore, the weight experiences more upward force in case ii and thereby goes up.

The phenomenon of bistability and snap-through mechanisms, as seen in tensegrity structures, is being explored as a way to generate electricity from ocean waves. How it could work in practice:

Imagine a buoy-type WEC that incorporates a tensegrity structure or a spring-loaded bistable mechanism.
 • Wave Interaction: As waves cause the buoy to heave (move up and down) or pitch (tilt), this motion would gradually load the bistable mechanism.
 • Energy Storage: Energy from the wave motion would be stored in the mechanism as potential energy (e.g., by deforming springs or changing the tensegrity configuration).
 • Snap-Through: Once a certain threshold of wave force or displacement is reached, the mechanism "snaps" into its alternative stable state.
 • Generator Activation: This rapid "snap" motion is then used to drive a power take-off (PTO) system.
